parse.title: Temperature regulation suppression
parse.wikitext:
<onlyinclude>
'''Temperature regulation suppression''' can be defined as an inability to maintain a normal temperature. This results in feelings of constantly fluctuating between being uncomfortably cold<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors=((Walsh, S.)), ((Strain, E.)), ((Abreu, M.)), ((Bigelow, G.)) | journal=Psychopharmacology | title=Enadoline, a selective kappa opioid agonist: comparison with butorphanol and hydromorphone in humans | volume=157 | issue=2 | pages=151–162 | date=1 September 2001 | url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/s002130100788 | issn=0033-3158 | doi=10.1007/s002130100788}}</ref> and uncomfortably hot. At points, this can even result in the sensation of being uncomfortably warm and cold simultaneously. 

Temperature regulation suppresion is often accompanied by other coinciding effects such as [[stimulation]] and [[increased perspiration]]. [[Serotonin]] is heavily implicated in thermoregulation, and as such It is most commonly induced under the influence of [[Serotonin#Serotonin system|serotonergic]] compounds, such as [[dosage#heavy|heavy]] [[dosage|dosages]] of [[Serotonergic psychedelic|serotonergic psychedelics]] compounds, such as [[LSD]], [[2C-B]], and [[AMT]]. However, it can also occur under the influence of [[stimulants]] such as [[amphetamines]], [[MDMA]] and [[cocaine]] through [[Dopamine|dopaminergic]] and [[adrenergic]] pathways affecting metabolic rate and, to some extent, serotonin.
</onlyinclude>
